claims.text: A physics-informed ML model using lattice-distortion scattering parameters and ab initio elastic and vibrational features will predict phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than empirical-descriptor models.
The target materials are equimolar, single-phase, four- or five-component FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys.
Arc melting followed by homogenization can produce the specified alloys without ordering or secondary phases.
Mass-fluctuation and strain-field descriptors can be derived from alloy composition.
DFT-computed elastic and vibrational features can be combined with compositional fluctuation descriptors to predict phonon thermal conductivity.
Lattice-distortion-induced phonon scattering is quantified by mass-fluctuation and strain-field variance parameters.
Multi-element disorder reduces phonon mean free path through lattice-distortion scattering.
Embedding physical scattering metrics in the ML feature set will capture disorder-induced reductions in phonon mean free path more accurately.
More accurate representation of disorder-induced phonon scattering will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error.
The physics-informed model will achieve a phonon-thermal-conductivity MAE of at most 0.7 W/m·K on a test set of equimolar HEAs.
The physics-informed model will improve prediction accuracy by at least 30% relative to the empirical-descriptor baseline.
A leading empirical-descriptor model has an MAE of approximately 1.0 W/m·K under the same conditions.
The proposed model is applicable from 300 to 800 K to equimolar, single-phase, four- or five-component FCC or BCC HEAs without significant ordering or phase separation.
The proposed model may not generalize to non-equimolar, ordered, or multiphase alloys.
Generalization to non-equimolar or ordered HEAs remains untested.
High-temperature anharmonic effects beyond 800 K remain untested.
The 3ω method can provide the required phonon thermal conductivity measurements from 300 to 800 K for the selected alloys.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if more than two of ten measured values differ from the physics-informed predictions by more than 15%.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if the empirical baseline attains an MAE of at most 0.7 W/m·K on the same test set.
